title: Do you think Bergman can cure my brain rot?

commenti.body:
May I ask what's making you think you have brain rot, and that you may find slower films challenging?

(The bot moderator just automatically deleted the above question because it wasn't long enough apparently, so I'm now going to add that you should try *The Magician* (1958) because I find it to be a "tighter" Bergman film, but also funnier and actually quite frightening with an excellent ending there I hope the bit doesn't delete this too if so I don't know what else to do good luck)

Thank you. Yeah for sure: I just cannot seem to focus that well anymore in movies. Now I’m too conscious of this issue as well so I’ll interrupt myself when I’m watching a movie (if that makes sense) 

Simply: I was planning on getting into Tatis films, I put on Mr Hulots holidays. I watched that and thought it’s quite funny but half the movie, when gags weren’t happening, I was off in my mind thinking about myself and things that have nothing to do with what was in front of me. 

It’s not that I have an inability to put my phone down, I can do that very happily and easily for a film (not sure about other things tho lol) but I feel like I’m used to multi tasking and that’s stopping me from truly getting into particular types of films. 

Apologies if this doesn’t make sense but thanks for the recommendation I’ll definitely give it a watch

Don’t watch Cries and Whispers imo. That one was painful for me, didn’t really have much going on visually. Unless you’re very interested in religious themes and death. Persona at least has some very impressive camera technique that makes it visually engaging while still retaining the classic, but still interesting, Bergman head scratching psychological slow plot

Surely if you already struggle to focus in films in general then you should probably work your way up from more exciting films to slower ones, rather than Han immediately going for the slowest ones possible?

I’m generally perfectly able to focus on films but I have struggled with some Bergman.

No, it all makes sense, thank you. Well, you seem pretty aware of yourself and that you're dissatisfied with finding lack of concentration challenging. That's a good thing obviously.

I was going to jump straight in and say it's your phone, but you got there first! I personally have challenges with concentration due to phone but also a two year-old who will not sleep. It sure takes its toll when I'd like to sit down for a couple of hours to watch a film.

All I find I can do is leave my phone in a different room, and stick the film on quite loud (or even with headphones, much more immersive. That generally engages me (if the kid wakes up, so be it, but it is improving).

If you're better at disciplining yourself with a phone, screen time, etc, then you're more disciplined than me. But I also think time away from a screen, social media, etc, means detox too. It needs to be put away for enough time for your head to be collected enough to begin a film let alone stick it out the whole way.

I personally enjoy *slower cinema*. I get the most from it. But from a cognitive perspective, it is the absolute antithesis of contemporary media culture, hence the brain not being sure which way to go. That's just my take, anyway. But yeah. *The Magician*. It's magnificent.

Yeah thanks but I only asked the question, though it may seem dumb, because maybe he will actually demand my entire attention (thoughts and eyes). The problem is just i have only noticed recently that things that aren’t mainstream generally don’t hold my attention well and i see myself having drifting thoughts.

Of all the complaints about Cries and Whispers, that it has not a lot going on visually is an odd one. It's one of the most visually stunning films I've seen. It won the Oscar for best cinematography that year and for good reason. I found it very engaging, I couldn't look away, there's a lot of 'what the fuck' moments and it lingered in my mind for days afterwards.

Thanks! I never thought of it like that but yes I should have a break from my phone before I watch, rather then putting it down and starting within a minute. 

Headphones is also a good idea so I’m definitely going to try that more often.

I might get a burner phone hahah

I’m just here scratching my head perplexed over this comment. Cries & Whispers is known and lauded for its *exquisite* cinematography and stark visual beauty. Sven Nykvist is an absolute genius cinematographer and the aesthetic he created for this film with the deep reds and greens is haunting and unforgettable.

Your brain does what it’s used to, nothing more and nothing less (ok, in the absence of neurodivergence blah blah blah). If you get expose yourself to slower things and spend more time doing ‘slow’ activities you’ll teach your brain to expect that.

Something that works for me is using my attention positively; intentionally doing something slow and paying extreme attention to it while I’m doing. You can make neuroscience arguments that this forces learning to happen and activates circuits that lead to a ‘quieter’ brain but all I know is that it makes me feel calmer and more comfortable being still.

You also don’t have to enjoy slow movies! It might be that you literally just don’t like them and that’s fine, but that you enjoy, say, fishing.
It makes complete sense bro, this happens with me too when I gets bored from a movie, first thing movie gotta do is to be properly paced and interesting everything comes secondary in my opinion.

Bergman's films will be likely be a challenge if you are more used to popcorny, crowd-pleasing blockbuster fair, but his films tend to be around 90 minutes, which will potentially make them easier to get through. It's definitely worth diving into his filmography as he truly is a master, but it's probably worth building up to his films rather than diving in the deep end.

I haven't seen his entire filmography, so I can't give you a definitive best entry point to his oeuvre, but of his films which I have seen, I'd say The Seventh Seal is a great place to start, as it surprisingly funny, which helps keep the audience engaged, plus provides a nice counterbalance the heavy themes.

A lot of people are having this issue due to short-form content and our general over reliance on technology. No specific movie or director is going to fix this for you. You need to develop enough willpower to overcome it yourself, e.g. spending less time on your phone, not having it in the same room, limiting the use of apps like TikTok or Instagram, forming new habits, etc.    
I recently went to the cinema to watch The Turin Horse and I’m glad I did because sitting through a three hour movie on my own is a struggle when there are so many distractions around me. It was one of the best experiences I’ve ever had, but guess what? The guy next to me was sat on his phone for the entirety of the movie after having paid £15 to attend. It was sad and honestly- really fucking annoying.    
So, the choice is yours. Do you want to be more present? Do you want to have experiences that are going to be difficult at first, but ultimately more meaningful than a fifteen second video? If so, you need to make a conscious decision every single day to do things differently.

Thanks! That’s why I think Bergman may be a solution because I’ll be forced to get comfortable on the slow stuff. Do you think I should? Or should I wait until I have a longer span to appreciate more?

I can understand the reasoning but I think the trouble is that with Bergman even if you do use your thought and your eyes fully, you may well still find that you just “don’t get it”, and that experience will be frustrating and off putting. (Of course experiences will vary but I think this is a pretty common experience).

I would suggest instead to either watch a film that is slow by modern standards but still exciting (such as a Sergio Leone film) or conversely one that requires lots of thought but is a bit more fast paced (such as 12 angry men).
